provenance.provenance_evidence: The project-owned projection passage reproduces the retained calendar body hash exactly. Its artifact manifest records the bounded public-domain 1862 Pustet antecedent, the separate 1962 target, and every editorial transformation; neither witness is represented as owning the projected bytes. The 1962 reading was established on that edition's page images rather than its text layer, cross-read against the Benziger conformed printing. Differences from the antecedent: 1862 sets a comma after 'turbae'; 1962 does not; THE MATERIAL ONE: 1862 closes 'Hosanna in excelsis.'; 1962 closes '« Hosanna ».' The 1962 drops two words from the acclamation and adds none; 1962 encloses the acclamation in guillemets. Corroboration: Venice 1570 at text-layer lines 24874-24880 and Vatican typica 1604 at text-layer lines 24776-24780, both read by eye at their Palm Sunday runs; both close 'Hosanna in excelsis'. So the longer close is the older reading in all three public-domain witnesses and the truncation is the 1955 book's.. Recorded limitation: THIS IS THE LANE'S CLOSEST CALL AND THE ONE MOST LIKELY TO BE OVERRULED. I called it matched on the criterion the guidance itself uses at guidance/propers-for-agents.md:360-363, where S. Petri Canisii was held back because part of the TARGET was uncorroborated ('the 1862 printed its opening clause and a different petition after it'). Here no part of the target is uncorroborated: every word the 1962 prints stands in the 1862 in the same order at the same place, and the 1955 book's only act was to cut two words, which contributes no new matter for 103(b) to reach. A reviewer applying the verdict list literally - 'an added or dropped clause' - would call this variant, and the difference is recorded above in full so that reclassifying it needs no re-reading. Confidence is set to medium for exactly that reason, and the reading itself is not in doubt on either side.

translations.caution:
A pre-1955 lay hand missal, not an approved liturgical translation and never an altar book. Its rubrics, its seasonal second and third orations, its Holy Week and its sanctoral are not those of 1962. It is carried only where a 1962 formulary is the same prayer, and nothing here may be used for recitation.

The 1862 prints the responsory `Ingrediente Domino in sanctam civitatem ... V. Cum audisset populus ...` at the return of the procession, identical to the 1962 index, and adds `Et non dicitur Gloria Patri.` The 1861 abbreviates the repeat as `&c. as above, to V.`, exactly as the Latin books cue it. Page-image collation confirms that this historical English body answers the complete target Latin identity; publication is limited to the 1861 wording and does not claim that Cummiskey appoints the 1962 celebration.

Its artifact manifest records the bounded public-domain 1862 Pustet antecedent, the separate 1962 target, and every editorial transformation; neither witness is represented as owning the projected bytes. The 1962 reading was established on that edition's page images rather than its text layer, cross-read against the Benziger conformed printing. This is the same collect the Roman Missal has carried since the 1570, and the 1955 reform did not touch it - it only moved it behind the procession rubrics. No 1862 page image exists for this leaf.
